entries.why_wrong: Speed isn't the issue here — `scanf` is plenty fast for reading a single word, and the program would still crash even if it ran instantly. The real problem is that `%s` has no length limit, so a 30-character word overruns the 16-byte `name` buffer and corrupts adjacent stack memory.

Zero-initializing `name` wouldn't help — the crash comes from writing too much data into it, not from reading stale bytes before it's filled. Even a fully zeroed 16-byte buffer still overflows once `scanf("%s", name)` writes a 30-character word into it.

`%d` is for reading integers, and `name` is a `char` array meant to hold text, so swapping to `%d` would just make `scanf` fail to parse a word at all — it wouldn't touch the actual bug. The overflow happens because `%s` has no width cap, letting input longer than 16 bytes overwrite memory past the buffer.
